items.stem: Which substance is an element?
items.answer: sulfur
items.markingKey: Sulfur contains only one type of atom.

items.stem: Which statement about a compound is correct?
options: Its properties are the average of the properties of its elements.
It contains two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
It can be separated into its elements by filtration.
items.answer: It contains two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
items.markingKey: Definition of a compound.

items.stem: Explain two differences between a mixture of iron and sulfur and the compound iron(II) sulfide.
items.answer: In the mixture iron and sulfur keep their properties (iron is magnetic, can be separated by a magnet) and can be in any ratio; in iron(II) sulfide they are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, with new properties, separable only by chemical reaction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: separation/properties; 1 mark: fixed vs variable ratio [2]

items.stem: A diagram of a box of particles shows two kinds of separate single atoms, not joined to each other. What does the box contain?
options: a single substance made of two elements that are not joined together
items.answer: a mixture
items.markingKey: Two kinds of separate single atoms, not joined to each other → mixture (two or more substances not chemically combined).

items.stem: Felix mixes 8.4 g of iron filings with 4.8 g of powdered sulfur and then heats part of the mixture strongly in a test tube. It glows red and forms a black solid, iron(II) sulfide. (a) Describe a test that shows the unheated sample is a mixture. (b) Classify iron, sulfur and iron(II) sulfide as elements or compounds.
items.answer: (a) Hold a magnet near it: iron is attracted and separated from the yellow sulfur. (b) iron and sulfur are elements; iron(II) sulfide is a compound
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: magnet; 1 mark: iron separated, sulfur left [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Which of these is a mixture?
items.answer: air
items.markingKey: Air contains N₂, O₂, Ar, CO₂ etc. not chemically combined.

items.stem: Explain why water is classified as a compound and not as a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.
items.answer: Hydrogen and oxygen atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (2:1); water has completely different properties from hydrogen and oxygen and cannot be separated by physical methods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: chemically combined fixed ratio; 1 mark: different properties / not separable physically [2]

items.stem: Explain why air is a mixture and not a compound.
items.answer: Its composition can vary, its components are not chemically combined and keep their own properties, and they can be separated physically (fractional distillation of liquid air).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two points [2]

items.stem: Two diagrams are drawn. Box 1 shows a mixture of compound molecules and element molecules. Box 2 shows two different kinds of molecule, each made of two identical atoms. Classify the contents of each box as an element, a compound or a mixture, giving a reason for each.
items.answer: Box 1: mixture; Box 2: mixture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Box 1 mixture with reason (two or more substances not chemically combined); 1 mark: Box 2 mixture with reason [2]

items.stem: In a water-testing laboratory, iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed and then heated. A teacher in Seoul uses 11.2 g of iron and 6.4 g of sulfur. (a) Describe a test that shows the unheated sample is a mixture. (b) Explain why the product cannot be separated by a magnet.
items.answer: (a) Hold a magnet near it: iron is attracted and separated from the yellow sulfur. (b) Iron and sulfur are chemically combined in iron(II) sulfide, which has different properties (not magnetic like iron).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: magnet; 1 mark: iron separated, sulfur left [2] (b) 1 mark: chemically combined; 1 mark: new properties [2]

items.stem: Which row shows the relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron?
items.answer: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
items.markingKey: Relative charges: p +1, n 0, e −1.

items.stem: Explain why the proton number, not the mass number, identifies an element.
items.answer: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons; the number of neutrons, and so the mass number, can differ (isotopes).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same protons for an element; 1 mark: neutrons/mass number can vary [2]

items.stem: Explain why a sodium ion, Na⁺, has a positive charge.
items.answer: A sodium atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons; it loses one electron to form Na⁺, so it has 11 protons and 10 electrons, giving an overall charge of +1.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loses one electron; 1 mark: one more proton than electrons [2]

items.stem: An ion of sodium is written as ²³₁₁Na⁺. Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
items.answer: protons 11, neutrons 12, electrons 10
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: protons = 11; neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12; electrons = 11 − 1 = 10 [3]

items.stem: An ion of magnesium is written as ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺. Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
items.answer: protons 12, neutrons 12, electrons 10
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: protons = 12; neutrons = 24 − 12 = 12; electrons = 12 − 2 = 10 [3]

items.stem: An ion of lithium is written as ⁷₃Li⁺. Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion. Explain why the ion has this charge.
items.answer: protons 3, neutrons 4, electrons 2; it has 1 more protons than electrons, so the charge is +1.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: protons = 3; neutrons = 7 − 3 = 4; electrons = 3 − 1 = 2 [3]; reason for charge [1]

items.stem: Chloe is studying magnesium, proton number 12, mass number 24. (a) Write the symbol of the atom showing its mass number and proton number. (b) Explain why the atom has no overall charge. (c) Magnesium forms the ion Mg²⁺. Deduce the number of electrons in this ion and explain how it forms.
items.answer: (a) ²⁴₁₂Mg (b) It has equal numbers of protons (12) and electrons (12), so the charges cancel. (c) 10 electrons; the atom loses 2 electron(s).
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark: number; 1 mark: lose/gain [2]

items.stem: Mohammed is studying beryllium, proton number 4, mass number 9. (a) State the relative mass and relative charge of each type of sub-atomic particle. (b) Another atom has 4 protons and 6 neutrons. State whether it is the same element and give its mass number.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) Yes, same element (same proton number); mass number 10; it is an isotope.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each particle [3] (b) 1 mark: same element; 1 mark: mass number [2]

items.stem: What is the relative mass of an electron?
items.answer: 1/1836 (almost zero)
items.markingKey: Electrons have negligible mass compared with protons and neutrons (relative mass 1).

items.stem: Compare an atom of chlorine-35 with a chloride ion formed from it, in terms of the numbers of sub-atomic particles.
items.answer: Both have 17 protons and 18 neutrons; the atom has 17 electrons, the ion has 18 electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same protons and neutrons; 1 mark: electrons 17 vs 18 [2]

items.stem: Explain why the mass of an atom is almost the same as the mass of its nucleus.
items.answer: Protons and neutrons each have relative mass 1, electrons have relative mass of only about 1/1836, so electrons add almost nothing to the mass.

items.stem: A student says, "The mass number is the number of particles in an atom." Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: Mass number counts only protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons are not included.

items.stem: How many electrons are there in the ion N³⁻? (Proton number of nitrogen = 7.)
items.markingKey: 7 protons; charge -3 → gained 3 electron(s): 7 − (-3) = 10.

items.stem: The table shows the numbers of sub-atomic particles in 3 particles. particle P: 4 protons, 5 neutrons, 4 electrons; particle Q: 10 protons, 10 neutrons, 10 electrons; particle R: 13 protons, 14 neutrons, 10 electrons. Identify each particle, writing its symbol with mass number, proton number and any charge.
items.answer: P is ⁹₄Be (atom); Q is ²⁰₁₀Ne (atom); R is ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺
items.markingKey: P is ⁹₄Be (atom); Q is ²⁰₁₀Ne (atom); R is ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺. Element from proton number; mass number = protons + neutrons; charge = protons − electrons. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The table shows the numbers of sub-atomic particles in 3 particles. particle P: 10 protons, 10 neutrons, 10 electrons; particle Q: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 17 electrons; particle R: 19 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons. Identify each particle, writing its symbol with mass number, proton number and any charge.
items.answer: P is ²⁰₁₀Ne (atom); Q is ³⁵₁₇Cl (atom); R is ³⁹₁₉K⁺
items.markingKey: P is ²⁰₁₀Ne (atom); Q is ³⁵₁₇Cl (atom); R is ³⁹₁₉K⁺. Element from proton number; mass number = protons + neutrons; charge = protons − electrons. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The table shows the numbers of sub-atomic particles in 3 particles. particle P: 20 protons, 20 neutrons, 20 electrons; particle Q: 1 protons, 1 neutrons, 1 electrons; particle R: 29 protons, 34 neutrons, 27 electrons. Identify each particle, writing its symbol with mass number, proton number and any charge.
items.answer: P is ⁴⁰₂₀Ca (atom); Q is ²₁H (atom); R is ⁶³₂₉Cu²⁺
items.markingKey: P is ⁴⁰₂₀Ca (atom); Q is ²₁H (atom); R is ⁶³₂₉Cu²⁺. Element from proton number; mass number = protons + neutrons; charge = protons − electrons. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The table shows the numbers of sub-atomic particles in 4 particles. particle P: 5 protons, 6 neutrons, 5 electrons; particle Q: 19 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons; particle R: 25 protons, 30 neutrons, 25 electrons; particle S: 14 protons, 14 neutrons, 14 electrons. Identify each particle, writing its symbol with mass number, proton number and any charge. State which particles, if any, are isotopes of the same element.
items.answer: P is ¹¹₅B (atom); Q is ³⁹₁₉K⁺; R is ⁵⁵₂₅Mn (atom); S is ²⁸₁₄Si (atom). Isotopes: none (no two have the same proton number but different mass numbers)
items.markingKey: P is ¹¹₅B (atom); Q is ³⁹₁₉K⁺; R is ⁵⁵₂₅Mn (atom); S is ²⁸₁₄Si (atom). Element from proton number; mass number = protons + neutrons; charge = protons − electrons. 1 mark each [4]; isotopes identified [1]

items.stem: Hana is studying fluorine, proton number 9, mass number 19. (a) State the relative mass and relative charge of each type of sub-atomic particle. (b) Write the symbol of the atom showing its mass number and proton number.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) ¹⁹₉F
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each particle [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Nadia is studying phosphorus, proton number 15, mass number 31. (a) State the relative mass and relative charge of each type of sub-atomic particle. (b) Write the symbol of the atom showing its mass number and proton number.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) ³¹₁₅P
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each particle [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: What are isotopes?
options: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
atoms of different elements with the same mass number
atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons
atoms with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
items.answer: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
items.markingKey: Isotopes: same proton number, different mass number.

items.stem: Explain why the relative atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5 even though no chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5.
items.answer: Ar is a weighted average of the masses of the isotopes (chlorine-35 about 75% and chlorine-37 about 25%), so it need not be a whole number.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weighted average of isotopes; 1 mark: abundances of Cl-35 and Cl-37 [2]

items.stem: Explain why chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 react in the same way with sodium.
items.answer: Both have 17 protons and 17 electrons with the same electronic configuration (2,8,7); chemical reactions involve electrons, so they react identically.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same electrons / configuration; 1 mark: reactions depend on electrons [2]

items.stem: A sample of gallium has the following isotopic composition: Ga-69: 60.1%; Ga-71: 39.9%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium to one decimal place.

Daniel, a student in Jakarta, is given data for the isotopes of silicon: Si-28: 92.2%; Si-29: 4.7%; Si-30: 3.1%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. Explain why the answer is not a whole number.
items.answer: 28.1; it is a weighted average of the masses of the isotopes.

items.stem: Amara is given data for a sample of element X: mass 32: 90%; mass 33: 10%. (a) Explain what is meant by the term isotopes. (b) Suggest one physical property that would differ between the isotopes. (c) Another sample of element X from a different source has a slightly higher relative atomic mass. Suggest an explanation.
items.answer: (a) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. (b) mass / density / rate of diffusion (of gaseous compounds) (c) It contains a higher proportion of the heavier isotope (33).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: same protons; 1 mark: different neutrons [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Why do isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties?
options: They have the same number of electrons in the outer shell (same electronic configuration).
They have the same number of neutrons.
items.answer: They have the same number of electrons in the outer shell (same electronic configuration).
items.markingKey: Chemical properties depend on electrons.

items.stem: Explain why the relative atomic mass of boron (10.8) is closer to 11 than to 10.
items.answer: Boron-11 is much more abundant (about 80%) than boron-10 (about 20%), so the weighted average is nearer 11.

items.stem: State and explain one physical property that differs between isotopes of an element.
items.answer: Mass/density (also rate of diffusion of gases): isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, so their atoms have different masses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property; 1 mark: different numbers of neutrons/mass [2]

items.stem: A sample of magnesium has the following isotopic composition: Mg-24: 79%; Mg-25: 10%; Mg-26: 11%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium to one decimal place.
A sample of chlorine has the following isotopic composition: Cl-35: 75%; Cl-37: 25%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine to one decimal place.
Antimony has two naturally occurring isotopes, Sb-121 and Sb-123. Its relative atomic mass is 121.86. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.

A mass spectrometer in Auckland analyses a sample of bromine. The results show these isotopes: mass 79: 50.7%; mass 81: 49.3%. (a) Explain what is meant by the term isotopes. (b) The proton number of bromine is 35. Give the number of neutrons in each isotope. (c) Suggest one physical property that would differ between the isotopes.
items.answer: (a) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. (b) 79: 44, 81: 46 (c) mass / density / rate of diffusion (of gaseous compounds)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: same protons; 1 mark: different neutrons [2] (b) neutrons = mass number − 35 [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons in the first shell of an atom?
items.markingKey: First shell holds up to 2 electrons; second and third up to 8 (for elements 1–20).

items.stem: Explain how the electronic configuration of an atom is linked to its position in the Periodic Table.
items.answer: The number of occupied shells gives the period number; the number of outer-shell electrons gives the group number (Group VIII has a full outer shell).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: shells → period; 1 mark: outer electrons → group [2]

items.stem: Explain why sodium and potassium have similar chemical reactions.
items.answer: Both have one electron in their outer shell (2,8,1 and 2,8,8,1), and reactions depend on outer-shell electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one outer electron each; 1 mark: chemistry depends on outer electrons [2]

items.stem: For each element, write the electronic configuration and state its group and period: beryllium (proton number 4), boron (proton number 5), fluorine (proton number 9).
items.answer: beryllium: 2,2, Group II, Period 2; boron: 2,3, Group III, Period 2; fluorine: 2,7, Group VII, Period 2
items.markingKey: beryllium: 2,2, Group II, Period 2; boron: 2,3, Group III, Period 2; fluorine: 2,7, Group VII, Period 2. 1 mark per element (configuration with group and period) [3]

items.stem: For each element, write the electronic configuration and state its group and period: aluminium (proton number 13), nitrogen (proton number 7), potassium (proton number 19).
items.answer: aluminium: 2,8,3, Group III, Period 3; nitrogen: 2,5, Group V, Period 2; potassium: 2,8,8,1, Group I, Period 4
items.markingKey: aluminium: 2,8,3, Group III, Period 3; nitrogen: 2,5, Group V, Period 2; potassium: 2,8,8,1, Group I, Period 4. 1 mark per element (configuration with group and period) [3]

items.stem: Priya is given element E, which has 11 protons in each atom. (a) Identify E. (b) Describe the arrangement of electrons in an atom of E in shells. (c) Predict the charge on the ion formed by E and give the configuration of this ion.
items.answer: (a) sodium (b) shell 1: 2, shell 2: 8, shell 3: 1 (c) +1; 2,8
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark charge; 1 mark configuration [2]

items.stem: Explain why helium is placed in Group VIII even though it has only two electrons in its outer shell.
items.answer: Its first (only) shell is full with two electrons, so like the other noble gases it has a stable full outer shell and is unreactive.

items.stem: A student says, "Chlorine is in Period 7 because it has seven outer electrons." Explain the error.
items.answer: Seven outer electrons means Group VII; chlorine (2,8,7) has three occupied shells so it is in Period 3.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 7 outer electrons = group; 1 mark: 3 shells = Period 3 [2]

items.stem: Explain why the elements in Period 2 all have two occupied electron shells but different chemical properties.
items.answer: They have the same number of shells but a different number of outer-shell electrons (1 to 8), and outer electrons determine chemical properties.

items.stem: Write the electronic configuration of the lithium atom (proton number 3) and of the ion Li⁺. Explain why the ion is stable.
items.answer: atom 2,1; ion 2 — the ion has a full outer shell like the noble gas helium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark atom 2,1; 1 mark ion 2; 1 mark full outer shell / noble gas configuration [3]

items.stem: Write the electronic configuration of the calcium atom (proton number 20) and of the ion Ca²⁺. Explain why the ion is stable.
items.answer: atom 2,8,8,2; ion 2,8,8 — the ion has a full outer shell like the noble gas argon.
items.markingKey: 1 mark atom 2,8,8,2; 1 mark ion 2,8,8; 1 mark full outer shell / noble gas configuration [3]

items.stem: Sipho is given element E, which has 16 protons in each atom. (a) State the group and period of E and explain how you deduced them. (b) Identify E.
items.answer: (a) Group VI, Period 3: 6 outer electrons and 3 occupied shells. (b) sulfur
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: group; 1 mark: period; 1 mark: reasoning [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Element E (proton number 4) is found in a mineral sample from Dubai. (a) Write the electronic configuration of an atom of E. (b) State the group and period of E and explain how you deduced them. (c) Identify E. (d) Describe the arrangement of electrons in an atom of E in shells.
items.answer: (a) 2,2 (b) Group II, Period 2: 2 outer electrons and 2 occupied shells. (c) beryllium (d) shell 1: 2, shell 2: 2
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark: group; 1 mark: period; 1 mark: reasoning [3] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Iron and sulfur powders are mixed. Which method separates the iron from the mixture?
items.answer: using a magnet
items.markingKey: Iron is magnetic; in a mixture each substance keeps its own properties.

items.stem: Explain why brass is described as a mixture even though it looks like a single metal.
items.answer: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; the metals are not chemically combined and the proportions can vary.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: alloy of Cu and Zn; 1 mark: not chemically combined / variable composition [2]

items.stem: Classify each of these as an element, a compound or a mixture: steel, nitrogen, sodium chloride, oxygen.
items.answer: steel: mixture; nitrogen: element; sodium chloride: compound; oxygen: element
items.markingKey: steel: mixture; nitrogen: element; sodium chloride: compound; oxygen: element. All 4 correct [2]; 3 or 2 correct [1] total [2]

items.stem: In a teaching laboratory, iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed and then heated. A teacher in Bangkok uses 2.8 g of iron and 1.6 g of sulfur. (a) Describe a test that shows the unheated sample is a mixture. (b) Explain why the product cannot be separated by a magnet. (c) Calculate the mass of iron(II) sulfide formed if all the iron and sulfur react. (d) Classify iron, sulfur and iron(II) sulfide as elements or compounds.
items.answer: (a) Hold a magnet near it: iron is attracted and separated from the yellow sulfur. (b) Iron and sulfur are chemically combined in iron(II) sulfide, which has different properties (not magnetic like iron). (c) 4.4 g (d) iron and sulfur are elements; iron(II) sulfide is a compound
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: magnet; 1 mark: iron separated, sulfur left [2] (b) 1 mark: chemically combined; 1 mark: new properties [2] (c) conservation of mass: 2.8 + 1.6 [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Where is most of the mass of an atom found?
items.answer: in the nucleus
items.markingKey: Protons and neutrons (mass 1 each) are in the nucleus.

items.stem: Kenji says that an atom of magnesium-24 (²⁴₁₂Mg) contains 24 neutrons. Explain Kenji's error and give the correct number of neutrons.
items.answer: The atom contains 12 neutrons: mass number − proton number = 24 − 12.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error explained; 1 mark: 12 neutrons [2]

items.stem: Jonas says that an atom of iron-56 (⁵⁶₂₆Fe) contains 56 neutrons. Explain Jonas's error and give the correct number of neutrons.
items.answer: The atom contains 30 neutrons: mass number − proton number = 56 − 26.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error explained; 1 mark: 30 neutrons [2]

items.stem: An ion of potassium is written as ³⁹₁₉K⁺. Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
items.answer: protons 19, neutrons 20, electrons 18
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: protons = 19; neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20; electrons = 19 − 1 = 18 [3]

items.stem: The table shows the numbers of sub-atomic particles in 3 particles. particle P: 19 protons, 20 neutrons, 19 electrons; particle Q: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 10 electrons; particle R: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 8 electrons. Identify each particle, writing its symbol with mass number, proton number and any charge.
items.answer: P is ³⁹₁₉K (atom); Q is ¹⁶₈O²⁻; R is ¹⁶₈O (atom)
items.markingKey: P is ³⁹₁₉K (atom); Q is ¹⁶₈O²⁻; R is ¹⁶₈O (atom). Element from proton number; mass number = protons + neutrons; charge = protons − electrons. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Grace is studying argon, proton number 18, mass number 40. (a) Give the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in one atom. (b) Explain why the atom has no overall charge.
items.answer: (a) 18 protons, 22 neutrons, 18 electrons (b) It has equal numbers of protons (18) and electrons (18), so the charges cancel.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Which pair of symbols represents two isotopes of the same element?
items.answer: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C
items.markingKey: Isotopes have the same proton number (6) but different mass numbers.

items.stem: A student says, "Isotopes are different elements because they have different mass numbers." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Isotopes have the same proton number, and the proton number defines the element; only the number of neutrons differs.

items.stem: Noah, a student in Doha, is given data for the isotopes of bromine: Br-79: 50.7%; Br-81: 49.3%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of bromine, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.

Felix, a student in Dubai, is given data for the isotopes of copper: Cu-63: 69.2%; Cu-65: 30.8%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. Explain why the answer is not a whole number.
items.answer: 63.6; it is a weighted average of the masses of the isotopes.

items.stem: Mohammed is given data for a sample of antimony: mass 121: 57.2%; mass 123: 42.8%. (a) The proton number of antimony is 51. Give the number of neutrons in each isotope. (b) Explain why the isotopes have identical chemical properties. (c) Another sample of antimony from a different source has a slightly higher relative atomic mass. Suggest an explanation.
items.answer: (a) 121: 70, 123: 72 (b) Same number and arrangement of electrons (same electronic configuration). (c) It contains a higher proportion of the heavier isotope (123).
items.markingKey: (a) neutrons = mass number − 51 [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Use electronic configurations to explain why sulfur (proton number 16) and oxygen (proton number 8) are in the same group but different periods.
items.answer: sulfur: 2,8,6; oxygen: 2,6. Both have 6 outer-shell electron(s), so same group (VI); they have 3 and 2 occupied shells, so different periods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both configurations; 1 mark: same outer electrons → same group; 1 mark: different number of shells → different period [3]

items.stem: Use electronic configurations to explain why boron (proton number 5) and aluminium (proton number 13) are in the same group but different periods.
items.answer: boron: 2,3; aluminium: 2,8,3. Both have 3 outer-shell electron(s), so same group (III); they have 2 and 3 occupied shells, so different periods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both configurations; 1 mark: same outer electrons → same group; 1 mark: different number of shells → different period [3]

items.stem: For each element, write the electronic configuration and state its group and period: silicon (proton number 14), sodium (proton number 11), magnesium (proton number 12).
items.answer: silicon: 2,8,4, Group IV, Period 3; sodium: 2,8,1, Group I, Period 3; magnesium: 2,8,2, Group II, Period 3
items.markingKey: silicon: 2,8,4, Group IV, Period 3; sodium: 2,8,1, Group I, Period 3; magnesium: 2,8,2, Group II, Period 3. 1 mark per element (configuration with group and period) [3]

items.stem: For each element, write the electronic configuration and state its group and period: beryllium (proton number 4), phosphorus (proton number 15), potassium (proton number 19).
items.answer: beryllium: 2,2, Group II, Period 2; phosphorus: 2,8,5, Group V, Period 3; potassium: 2,8,8,1, Group I, Period 4
items.markingKey: beryllium: 2,2, Group II, Period 2; phosphorus: 2,8,5, Group V, Period 3; potassium: 2,8,8,1, Group I, Period 4. 1 mark per element (configuration with group and period) [3]

items.stem: Felix is given element E, which has 6 protons in each atom. (a) State the group and period of E and explain how you deduced them. (b) Identify E. (c) Describe the arrangement of electrons in an atom of E in shells.
items.answer: (a) Group IV, Period 2: 4 outer electrons and 2 occupied shells. (b) carbon (c) shell 1: 2, shell 2: 4
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: group; 1 mark: period; 1 mark: reasoning [3] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Define the term element.
items.answer: A substance made up of only one type of atom (cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means).

items.stem: A student says, "Sodium chloride is a mixture of sodium and chlorine." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Sodium chloride is a compound: sodium and chlorine are chemically combined (ionic bonding) in a fixed 1:1 ratio, and it has different properties from either element.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: compound, chemically combined; 1 mark: fixed ratio / new properties [2]

items.stem: Classify each of these as an element, a compound or a mixture: nitrogen, calcium carbonate, sulfuric acid (pure), ink.
items.answer: nitrogen: element; calcium carbonate: compound; sulfuric acid (pure): compound; ink: mixture
items.markingKey: nitrogen: element; calcium carbonate: compound; sulfuric acid (pure): compound; ink: mixture. All 4 correct [2]; 3 or 2 correct [1] total [2]

items.stem: In a school laboratory, iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed and then heated. A teacher in Bangkok uses 5.6 g of iron and 3.2 g of sulfur. (a) Describe a test that shows the unheated sample is a mixture. (b) Calculate the mass of iron(II) sulfide formed if all the iron and sulfur react. (c) State two differences between the mixture and the compound. (d) Classify iron, sulfur and iron(II) sulfide as elements or compounds.
items.answer: (a) Hold a magnet near it: iron is attracted and separated from the yellow sulfur. (b) 8.8 g (c) Mixture: components keep their properties / any ratio / separable physically. Compound: fixed ratio / new properties / separated only chemically. (d) iron and sulfur are elements; iron(II) sulfide is a compound
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: magnet; 1 mark: iron separated, sulfur left [2] (b) conservation of mass: 5.6 + 3.2 [1] (c) 1 mark each [2] (d) [1]

items.stem: What is the mass number of an atom?
options: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
the number of protons and electrons
items.answer: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
items.markingKey: Mass number (nucleon number) = protons + neutrons.

items.stem: Diego says that an atom of argon-40 (⁴⁰₁₈Ar) contains 22 protons. Explain Diego's error and give the correct number of protons.
items.answer: The atom contains 18 protons: the proton number, 18.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error explained; 1 mark: 18 protons [2]

items.stem: Nadia says that an atom of sulfur-32 (³²₁₆S) contains 16 protons. Explain Nadia's error and give the correct number of protons.
items.answer: The atom contains 16 protons: the proton number, 16.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error explained; 1 mark: 16 protons [2]

items.stem: An ion of sulfur is written as ³²₁₆S²⁻. Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
items.answer: protons 16, neutrons 16, electrons 18
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: protons = 16; neutrons = 32 − 16 = 16; electrons = 16 + 2 = 18 [3]

items.stem: An ion of zinc is written as ⁶⁴₃₀Zn²⁺. Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
items.answer: protons 30, neutrons 34, electrons 28
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: protons = 30; neutrons = 64 − 30 = 34; electrons = 30 − 2 = 28 [3]

items.stem: Noah is studying argon, proton number 18, mass number 40. (a) Explain why almost all the mass of the atom is in the nucleus. (b) Another atom has 18 protons and 23 neutrons. State whether it is the same element and give its mass number.
items.answer: (a) Protons and neutrons (relative mass 1 each) are in the nucleus; electrons have negligible mass. (b) Yes, same element (same proton number); mass number 41; it is an isotope.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark: same element; 1 mark: mass number [2]

items.stem: Which pair of symbols represents two isotopes of the same element?
items.answer: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴²₁₈Ar
items.markingKey: Isotopes have the same proton number (18) but different mass numbers.

items.stem: Gallium has isotopes including Ga-69 and Ga-71, and its relative atomic mass is 69.8. Explain what the isotopes have in common, how they differ, and why the Ar is closest to 69.
items.answer: Same number of protons (31) and electrons; different numbers of neutrons (38 and 40); Ga-69 is the most abundant isotope (60.1%), so the weighted average is nearest 69.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same protons/electrons; 1 mark: different neutrons with numbers; 1 mark: most abundant isotope dominates the weighted average [3]

items.stem: Amara, a student in Lagos, is given data for the isotopes of europium: Eu-151: 47.8%; Eu-153: 52.2%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of europium, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
Bromine has two naturally occurring isotopes, Br-79 and Br-81. Its relative atomic mass is 79.99. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.

Sofia is given data for a sample of element X: mass 30: 62%; mass 31: 38%. (a) Explain what is meant by the term isotopes. (b) Suggest one physical property that would differ between the isotopes. (c) Another sample of element X from a different source has a slightly higher relative atomic mass. Suggest an explanation.
items.answer: (a) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. (b) mass / density / rate of diffusion (of gaseous compounds) (c) It contains a higher proportion of the heavier isotope (31).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: same protons; 1 mark: different neutrons [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Use electronic configurations to explain why argon (proton number 18) and neon (proton number 10) are in the same group but different periods.
items.answer: argon: 2,8,8; neon: 2,8. Both have 8 outer-shell electron(s), so same group (VIII); they have 3 and 2 occupied shells, so different periods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both configurations; 1 mark: same outer electrons → same group; 1 mark: different number of shells → different period [3]

items.stem: Use electronic configurations to explain why oxygen (proton number 8) and sulfur (proton number 16) are in the same group but different periods.
items.answer: oxygen: 2,6; sulfur: 2,8,6. Both have 6 outer-shell electron(s), so same group (VI); they have 2 and 3 occupied shells, so different periods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both configurations; 1 mark: same outer electrons → same group; 1 mark: different number of shells → different period [3]

items.stem: Write the electronic configuration of the fluorine atom (proton number 9) and of the ion F⁻. Explain why the ion is stable.
items.answer: atom 2,7; ion 2,8 — the ion has a full outer shell like the noble gas neon.
items.markingKey: 1 mark atom 2,7; 1 mark ion 2,8; 1 mark full outer shell / noble gas configuration [3]

items.stem: For each element, write the electronic configuration and state its group and period: neon (proton number 10), oxygen (proton number 8), carbon (proton number 6).
items.answer: neon: 2,8, Group VIII, Period 2; oxygen: 2,6, Group VI, Period 2; carbon: 2,4, Group IV, Period 2
items.markingKey: neon: 2,8, Group VIII, Period 2; oxygen: 2,6, Group VI, Period 2; carbon: 2,4, Group IV, Period 2. 1 mark per element (configuration with group and period) [3]

items.stem: Sofia is given element E, which has 11 protons in each atom. (a) Name another element with similar chemical properties to E and explain why. (b) Describe the arrangement of electrons in an atom of E in shells. (c) Predict the charge on the ion formed by E and give the configuration of this ion.
items.answer: (a) any element in Group I (same number of outer electrons) (b) shell 1: 2, shell 2: 8, shell 3: 1 (c) +1; 2,8
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: element; 1 mark: same number of outer electrons [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark charge; 1 mark configuration [2]
